title: Linear equations and consistent systems
section: Solutions of Linear Systems ▷ Consistency and Number of Solutions
terms: linear equation; linear system; coefficient; unknown; solution; consistent system; inconsis- tent system.

exposition.text:
A linear equation has the form a x + · · · + a x = b with fixed coefficients. A linear system asks
1 1 n n
for a single vector satisfying every equation. It is consistent if it has at least one solution and
inconsistent otherwise. Over R or C, a linear system has zero, one, or infinitely many solutions.
If u, v are two distinct solutions, every (1 − t)u + tv is also a solution, giving infinitely many.
A system with fewer equations than unknowns need not be consistent, but if it is consistent it
cannot have a unique solution. The zero-one-infinity statement depends on the infinite scalar
field: over a finite field, a system can have a finite number greater than one.

question.text:
For which (a, b) does the system x + y + z = 1, 2x + 2y + 2z = a, x − y = b have infinitely many
real solutions?
(A) a = 2, any b (B) a = 2, b = 0 (C) a = 1, any b (D) Any a, b = 0 (E) No such pair

solution.text:
The second equation is compatible with the first exactly when a = 2. The first and third
equations are independent and then leave one free variable, for every real b.

question.text:
A real system Ax = b has two distinct solutions u, v. Which vector must also be a solution?
(A) u + v (B) 2u (C) 3u − 2v (D) u − v (E) 0

solution.text:
A(3u − 2v) = 3b − 2b = b. The coefficients sum to one. None of the other choices has this
guarantee when b ̸= 0.

question.text:
For a system of two linear equations in four real unknowns, which list gives all possible num-
bers of solutions as the coefficients and constants vary?
(A) 0 or 1 only
(B) 1 or infinitely many only
(C) Infinitely many only
(D) 0 or infinitely many only
(E) 0, 1, or infinitely many

solution.text:
Inconsistency is possible, for example with equations x = 0 and x = 1. If the system
1 1
is consistent, its rank is at most two, so at least two of the four unknowns are free. It
therefore has infinitely many solutions, never exactly one.
